content.text:
Jeffrey Lorenger
Chairman, President, and CEO, HNI
Thanks, Marshall. In closing, we are well-positioned for both the current environment and the long term. In Workplace Furnishings, our profit improvement actions will continue to drive results. Our future profit growth is not dependent on volume. However, we expect demand to eventually benefit from employment shifts, population migration, and the accelerated adoption of hybrid work models. These trends all align with our strong market positions. We are excited about our soon-to-be combination with Kimball International. The complementary nature of the businesses will create compelling value for all of our stakeholders. In Residential Building Products, while we are prepared for weak near-term demand, we remain focused on driving long-term growth. The high margin, high return businesses possess market leading brands, unmatched product depth and price point breadth, and unequaled distribution capabilities.
Its vertically integrated model and regional distribution infrastructure will continue to provide superior customer service and support for our market leadership positions. We will now open the call to your questions.
Operator
Thank you. At this time, I would like to remind everyone, in order to ask a question, press star, then the number 1 on your telephone keypad. We'll take our first question from Budd Bugatch at Water Tower Research.
Budd Bugatch
Head of Consumer Hardline Equity Research, Water Tower Research
Good morning, Jeff. Good morning, Marshall and Matt, and congratulations on good performance for Q1. I think one of the things that really raised my eyebrows was the 13% order growth in Workplace Furnishings, which, when you compare that to the results reported by BIFMA, at least so far to date in 2023, was much higher than what the industry looks like. Is there some explanation for that? Can you provide color? Was it because of March? BIFMA hasn't yet completed March. Can you give us any thoughts on that?
Jeffrey Lorenger
Chairman, President, and CEO, HNI
Yeah, Budd, this is Jeff. First, I would say what pertains to BIFMA, I think what we've kind of witnessed over our years is it will bounce around a bit quarter to quarter. Everyone does price increases at a different time, and there's lag there. I don't get too caught up on the BIFMA numbers on a point in time, but maybe over a longer time period it's a little more accurate to compare. I would say for us, we continue to see strength in the mid-market, in the SMB portion of the mid-market, and that surprised us a bit. In the contract side, I think what you saw, both of those segments benefited from some price increase pull ahead, but we also were encouraged because we see customers were close to pulling the trigger.
We recall a lot of customers have been sitting on the sidelines in a planning mode, and I think it forced them to make decisions and move. From an overall industry standpoint, I think that was a really good sign, for us anyway, to see that customers were close enough and were willing to make the investments.
Budd Bugatch
Head of Consumer Hardline Equity Research, Water Tower Research
Thank you. A little bit maybe a little further into that. We've heard from others that there's a lot of activity, but it's taking longer to bring that to fruition. You also made a comment that you had pricing pull forward, and that would imply that there were price increases that were actually happening during Q1. Otherwise, the pull forward would have been ahead of that. Am I have that right? You said SMid and contract were about the similar rates, and just want to make sure I understand why you think that might be that way.
Jeffrey Lorenger
Chairman, President, and CEO, HNI
Budd, I think our price increase went into effect 1 March. I think it did occur in the quarter. I think we did see an impact from the price increase.
Budd Bugatch
Head of Consumer Hardline Equity Research, Water Tower Research
How much was that, Jeff? What does it look like overall?
Jeffrey Lorenger
Chairman, President, and CEO, HNI
I'd say overall, when you kind of net it all up, about 50% we probably attribute to pull forward ahead of a price increase. We got historical benchmarks we look at, and we're obviously in a bit of a unique position, but that's our best guess, 50%.
Budd Bugatch
Head of Consumer Hardline Equity Research, Water Tower Research
You think 6.5% of the delta thereabouts was due to the price increase?
Jeffrey Lorenger
Chairman, President, and CEO, HNI
Yes. That's a fair way to say it.
Budd Bugatch
Head of Consumer Hardline Equity Research, Water Tower Research
Okay. My second question is that, again, the performance in RBP, certainly the profit performance is certainly notable. There's demand issues in the quarter. A couple of things surprised me on that. One, that it looks like remodel/retrofit was impacted more than new housing construction, because I thought that would, in what we've seen with interest rates and mortgage rates, I would have thought new housing would have been more impacted. Secondly, usually in a time like this when others are bruised, or when you're bruised, others are pretty much hemorrhaging, so there might be more opportunities to acquire in that. Do you see that? If there are, does the Kimball acquisition say, My appetite might not be so good at this point in time?
Jeffrey Lorenger
Chairman, President, and CEO, HNI
Yeah, Budd, let me parse that. There's a lot there. I would say, first of all, I'd start with, and I always start with, we continue to invest through this in RBP. We tend to find, with our leading categories and leading positions, investments to grow the category work out well for us, and we pick up a disproportionate share on any expansion from our position. That's a good thing. On your question around R&R, I think for the year, I would say we still anticipate that new construction will be worse than R&R for the year. In the quarter, I think we saw we have an early buy program that impacts R&R. The assumption we made, basically, the trade didn't take advantage of it as much as they have in the past.
Particularly, I think it's a phenomenon around lead times and are getting back to normal and not hoarding product like they were kind of gotten to a mental state of doing that for the last couple of years. That impacted the quarter in R&R, I think, and that's a little bit distorted. Overall, we believe new construction for the year will still be down more than R&R.
Budd Bugatch
Head of Consumer Hardline Equity Research, Water Tower Research
Got you. Okay.
Jeffrey Lorenger
Chairman, President, and CEO, HNI
I think you had another question in there that what was it? Yeah. Did I miss anything?
Budd Bugatch
Head of Consumer Hardline Equity Research, Water Tower Research
Yeah. With the idea of others being hurt.
Jeffrey Lorenger
Chairman, President, and CEO, HNI
Oh
Budd Bugatch
Head of Consumer Hardline Equity Research, Water Tower Research
What's your view of pipeline of transactions and maybe potential acquisitions in that? You've been mostly acquiring, at least in the last couple of years, distribution. Is that something that you see continuing or are there opportunities in that space?
Jeffrey Lorenger
Chairman, President, and CEO, HNI
Yeah, Budd, good question. I think we continue, we'll always be on the lookout in that space, I don't think our posture will change post-acquisition versus what it was pre-acquisition.
Budd Bugatch
Head of Consumer Hardline Equity Research, Water Tower Research
Okay. Thank you. I'll take two more and then defer. If we can get walkthroughs of maybe the year-over-year changes in gross profit and for SG&A, if Marshall can give us maybe some quantification of what may be the major components of change in gross margin and SG&A margin.
Marshall Bridges
SVP and CFO, HNI
Yeah, happy to do that, Budd. As it relates to gross profit margin, we saw about 160 basis points of headwind from volume. Lower volume was a negative impact. We were able to more than offset that with a favorable price cost, which added about 130 basis points, and the impact of our cost savings program, which added about 100 basis points. Think of that as productivity. Then we had maybe 3 other categories, which added about 140 basis points collectively. They included the divestiture of Lamex, some product mix, and some program changes. All in, we saw 210 points of gross profit margin expansion on a non-GAAP basis.
Budd Bugatch
Head of Consumer Hardline Equity Research, Water Tower Research
Got you.
Marshall Bridges
SVP and CFO, HNI
As it relates to SG&A. Oh, go ahead. Sorry.
Budd Bugatch
Head of Consumer Hardline Equity Research, Water Tower Research
SG&A, the same way. I'm sorry. I apologize.
Marshall Bridges
SVP and CFO, HNI
Yeah. This one's a little bit of a simpler story. We did see SG&A as percent of sales increase, and it really is driven by the volume decline, partially offset by our cost reduction program, which reduced SG&A dollars by about $5 million in the quarter.
Budd Bugatch
Head of Consumer Hardline Equity Research, Water Tower Research
Got you. Okay. I'll defer for others, and thank you for taking my questions.
Jeffrey Lorenger
Chairman, President, and CEO, HNI
Thanks, Budd.
Operator
We'll move to our next question from Reuben Garner at Benchmark Company.
Reuben Garner
Equity Research Analyst, Benchmark Company
Thank you. Good morning, everybody.
Jeffrey Lorenger
Chairman, President, and CEO, HNI
Morning.
Reuben Garner
Equity Research Analyst, Benchmark Company
The price increase in Workplace Furnishings that went into effect 1 March, I guess, one, is that something that you're seeing across the industry? Was that specific to one side of your workplace business? Meaning the small business channel, or was that both in contract and small business? The second part of the question is, what have order trends looked like since that increase went into place in March and April? If you could help with more recent trends.
Jeffrey Lorenger
Chairman, President, and CEO, HNI
Yeah. Reuben, I think the price increase is kind of our generic across the board. We look at it year over year, look at cost inputs, and make the best determination. It was not specific to one category of the business or one segment of the business. Since the price increase, what we've seen is still First of all, orders throughout the quarter sequentially got better. Second of all, the mid-market, we still see our five-week, most recent, is still up low single digits. The transactional piece of the SMB, which is a smaller piece of our businesses, continues to be weak. The contract is flattish to prior year right now on the recent five-week average.
Marshall Bridges
SVP and CFO, HNI
Reuben, maybe just to add to that. This is your typical normalization pattern you see post-price increase, and we're starting to get up against last year's price increase. There's a lot of noise in the system right now. Generally speaking, things have behaved like you would think they would after a price increase.
Reuben Garner
Equity Research Analyst, Benchmark Company
Okay. Yeah, no, flattest year-over-year is pretty encouraging, I think, in this environment. I guess that speaks to where you guys are in the market. Maybe on the Hearth product side, can you talk to me about how we should think about margins as they progress through the year? Are the productivity savings, are they kind of tilted more towards one of your businesses than the other? I'm just asking if your Workplace business is kind of running flat year-over-year and there's a little bit more pressure in Hearth, does that allow you to get more done from a productivity standpoint in the Hearth segment?
Marshall Bridges
SVP and CFO, HNI
Look, Reuben, if you look at our cost savings program, we're expecting about $35 million of benefit on the year. That is going to impact both segments, and it's really split about 60% Workplace and 40% Residential Building Products, and that also includes the benefit of price cost. The net result of that is we're going to see Workplace grow profit and margin this year, and we're going to see some compression in Residential Building Products, just maybe not as much as you might expect. I'm not sure if that answers your question.
Reuben Garner
Equity Research Analyst, Benchmark Company
No, that's helpful. I guess I was wondering about the progression for margins. The comps are choppy on the top line as we go through the year. Do you expect the kind of margins that we saw in Q1 to be the right way of looking at the business as the year progresses?
Marshall Bridges
SVP and CFO, HNI
In Residential Building Products, we'll see margin changes more to the seasonal volume. No, Q1's a decent quarter, right? Remember, Q2 is the seasonal trough, then we build our way back up. You're going to see different margins by quarter. Now, I don't think the Q1's a great read on the rest of the year. It never is.
Reuben Garner
Equity Research Analyst, Benchmark Company
Okay. I'm going to sneak one more in. Sorry to bounce around, I'm going to go back to Workplace for a second. I think I either heard or read that the trends in SMB continue to be better than contract. Is that right? Thank you for the detail on the most recent five weeks by segment. Did they look similar in Q1 relative to each other, transactional SMB and contract?
Marshall Bridges
SVP and CFO, HNI
Yeah. In Q1, SMB was up in the high teens and contract was up in the mid-teens. They are pretty similar. The SMB was a bit stronger. When you look into SMB, we saw the same pattern we have been seeing for six, nine months, where the mid-market was strong and the transactional business was weak. They averaged out to be up in the high teens.
Reuben Garner
Equity Research Analyst, Benchmark Company
Is the transactional piece weak? Is that just tied to the macro uncertainty? Is that something bigger than that? Has that business historically been a leading indicator for what you can expect in the other, in the more of the project space on a go-forward basis?
Marshall Bridges
SVP and CFO, HNI
I'm not sure it's a great read given that we've had such a unique situation from the pandemic. Yes, we do believe the transactional business is being impacted by the macroeconomic conditions. These are small purchases that are easy to defer when you're worried about cost. I'm not sure it necessarily is indicative of a future problem in the other segments, right? We've got a lot of pent-up demand out there from several years of employment growing faster than industry shipments, which seems like at some point needs to catch up.
Reuben Garner
Equity Research Analyst, Benchmark Company
Okay, great. Congrats on the results, guys, and good luck going forward.
Jeffrey Lorenger
Chairman, President, and CEO, HNI
Thanks, Reuben.
Operator
We'll go next to Greg Burns at Sidoti & Company.
Greg Burns
Analyst, Sidoti & Company
Morning. Just wanted to, I guess, touch on the, I guess, positive trends you're seeing in the Workplace Furnishings segment. When you look at what's been going on more recently with decisions being delayed and maybe spending being halted, maybe for macro or for other reasons. The inflection or the change you saw this quarter, what gives you confidence that that might be more of a change or a change in trend versus maybe a one-off thing? Are you seeing your funnel fill, your pipeline of business increasing? Is there any kind of forward-looking indicators that might give us confidence that this is maybe the beginning of an inflection in the industry?
Jeffrey Lorenger
Chairman, President, and CEO, HNI
Yeah, that's a good question, Greg. Look, it's encouraging. Our activity levels are high. It's encouraging that people have got off the sidelines. What I would say, long-term trends, I think we're seeing some signs of positivity there. Inflection point may be a little muted, though, I would say, just given the economic cycle we're in. I think it's encouraging that even though some of the headline news is pretty gloom and doom, we saw some pretty nice activity and our customers are pretty active. I think that's indicative of just, we've been in this holding pattern for quite some time, and people, although we may see some short-term economic pause, people are realizing that they want to move forward, and they can't stay in a holding pattern forever. I think that piece of this is a positive, and I think bodes well for the future.
Greg Burns
Analyst, Sidoti & Company
Okay. In terms of the price increase, it seems like inflation's kind of cooling down a little bit, and you've caught up in terms of price cost. Is that just your natural every year price increase that you put in? What's the rationale behind raising price again here at this point? Is there any risk that the market won't accept pricing going higher from here?
Marshall Bridges
SVP and CFO, HNI
Well, Greg, I think the thing to recognize is that inflation hasn't gone away. It's just become reduced. We're still seeing inflation. We're expecting inflation in the neighborhood of $10 to $20 million this year. We're going to offset that with pricing, some of which was carried over from last year, and some of which is from the new price increases. As far as their acceptance so far, we're seeing pretty reasonable acceptance across the board, as you might expect, given the industry conditions.
Jeffrey Lorenger
Chairman, President, and CEO, HNI
Yeah, I would say, Greg, that to your first part of the question, we're back in line to a more normal cycle price increase. We do have, as Marshall said, it's not headline news as much as it was, but we can tell you it's still out there. With this, I would call this more of a typical price increase, not something that was meant to catch up or plug holes.
Greg Burns
Analyst, Sidoti & Company
Okay. All right, great. Thanks.
Jeffrey Lorenger
Chairman, President, and CEO, HNI
Yep.
Operator
We'll take our next question from Steven Ramsey at Thompson Research Group.
Steven Ramsey
Deputy Director of Research, Thompson Research Group
Good morning. Wanted to ask a question, Workplace orders being strong ahead of the pricing, was it enough pull ahead to limit the margin outlook for the rest of the year in a meaningful way, given you may not get as full of a benefit of the pricing in the next few months?
Marshall Bridges
SVP and CFO, HNI
No, Steven, we don't see any material impact from that. I do understand your point, but it wasn't enough to make a big difference on the year, and we feel confident in our profit improvement actions are going to deliver profit growth in Workplace for the year.
Steven Ramsey
Deputy Director of Research, Thompson Research Group
Okay. Helpful. Thinking in Workplace on your advantages and long-term strengths in the SMB vertical, are you seeing an increase of competition in that vertical from other players?
Jeffrey Lorenger
Chairman, President, and CEO, HNI
That's a good question, Steven. What I would say about that is, look, that space is always competitive. It's been competitive and it will remain competitive. We've spent years tuning our model for that space with our selling and fulfillment capabilities. We've been competing there for decades against a wide array, big, large, and medium competitors, product-specific competitors. I wouldn't say we've really seen anything other than business as usual, and we're going to continue to invest in our model to maintain our leadership position.
Steven Ramsey
Deputy Director of Research, Thompson Research Group
Okay. Helpful. Another one on Workplace. Recent results at Kimball. Curious what your view of their results were. It seems like solid sales, but order rates even better. Broadly, just curious if you have a view on their results and maybe how they read into the marketplace that you're looking at.
Marshall Bridges
SVP and CFO, HNI
I think their story is fairly similar to what we're saying, Steven. We're both making good progress on the cost and margin side. We're not really in a position to provide additional detail on their results right now.
Steven Ramsey
Deputy Director of Research, Thompson Research Group
Okay. Helpful. Last one from me, thinking long term on the RBP segment, margins were in the 18% to 19% range in 2018 through 2022. Softer patch maybe this year. Thinking about the actions you're taking and the new products displayed at KBIS a few months ago, do you think 18% to 19% is the low area or even better when you get to the other side of 2023?
Marshall Bridges
SVP and CFO, HNI
Yeah, Steven, if you remember, our main strategy kind of battle cry in that segment is to maintain our strong margins. We're referring to the margins we had before this year and really drive top-line growth. Yeah, I think we can absolutely get back to where we were and more importantly, drive the top line beyond where we were over the intermediate to long term.
Steven Ramsey
Deputy Director of Research, Thompson Research Group
Okay, helpful. Thank you.
Operator
We'll take a follow-up from Budd Bugatch at Water Tower Research.
Budd Bugatch
Head of Consumer Hardline Equity Research, Water Tower Research
Yeah. Thank you for that. Just to clarify what you were talking about with Steven a moment ago. I think if I understood Jeff right, about half of the delta between for RBP's profit performance in Q1 was due to the profit improvement actions, and that would imply, I think it was a 270 basis point differential between this year and last year in the operating margin for that. Is that the right way to understand that?
Marshall Bridges
SVP and CFO, HNI
Yes, Budd. For the year, we expect some pretty severe pressure on the top line, and we expect to offset about half or maybe a little more than half of that pressure with our profit improvement actions. Basically, Residential Building Products share of that $85 to $95 million of profit support that we mentioned earlier.
Budd Bugatch
Head of Consumer Hardline Equity Research, Water Tower Research
Okay. You did talk about 80% of the profitability of the company will be in H2. Is there any major difference in segment? Are they both in the same kind of relative positioning?
Marshall Bridges
SVP and CFO, HNI
No. That's an average, right? The 80% of non-GAAP EPS being driven in the H2 of the year obviously accounts for both segments. We typically see more seasonality in Workplace. Last year, 75% of Workplace's non-GAAP operating income was in the H2. We expect it to be more in the 90% plus range this year. Residential Building Products is a little less seasonal on a H1, H2 basis. They were 52% last year, expect them to be more in the 60% range this year.
Budd Bugatch
Head of Consumer Hardline Equity Research, Water Tower Research
Okay. That makes sense to me. Just talking about the Kimball acquisition, to the extent you can, and if you can't, I understand that because it's still there, are there any surprises so far in the due diligence? What about the expectation for reporting structure? Any changes in the way you think you'll report segments?
Jeffrey Lorenger
Chairman, President, and CEO, HNI
Yeah, Budd. No surprises. I would say, just in response to your question, we are receiving very positive commentary from the trade and dealers confirming our thesis around the transaction. That's, I think, been encouraging as well. On reporting, we're really not in a position other than to say what we've already announced, which is the three primary commercial leaders in that business will report to me. That's all we've said at this point.
Budd Bugatch
Head of Consumer Hardline Equity Research, Water Tower Research
I was actually thinking about the accounting structure and the accounting reporting. I'm sorry. I didn't mean to imply anything in the organizational people. I was thinking that we now have Workplace Furnishings and RBP. Is it all going to go into RBP, or how do you look at that?
Marshall Bridges
SVP and CFO, HNI
Yeah, we'll still have two segments, Budd. That's our expectation. The Kimball International business is very similar to our Workplace Furnishings business. That would be accounted for under one segment.
Budd Bugatch
Head of Consumer Hardline Equity Research, Water Tower Research
Okay. Finally from me, you did file a new 425 this morning, and I realize that the SEC's got specific, but if I read it right, it's simply the same as the 8-K. Was there anything different in the 425 filed this morning than just the requirement that the communication be having that label?
Marshall Bridges
SVP and CFO, HNI
Correct. Anytime we mention or refer to the Kimball International or the transaction, we have to include it in the Form 425 filing. Even if it has a separate 8-K or other document, it has to go in the Form 425. You've seen the press release come out today, under both forms, and you've also seen some other kind of small communication items come out on the Form 425, none of which change anything related to the deal.
Budd Bugatch
Head of Consumer Hardline Equity Research, Water Tower Research
Okay. Will you update guidance once the acquisition is done, or will we just wait for the next quarter?
Marshall Bridges
SVP and CFO, HNI
I think, Budd, we're contemplating having more commentary on that on our next earnings call and not having a special announcement. We'll take that into consideration and see what we need to do.
Budd Bugatch
Head of Consumer Hardline Equity Research, Water Tower Research
Okay. The Q, when will the Q be filed? The expectation for that?
Marshall Bridges
SVP and CFO, HNI
Our Q will be filed tomorrow.
Budd Bugatch
Head of Consumer Hardline Equity Research, Water Tower Research
Okay. Marshall and Jeff, congratulations on the quarter. Thank you for taking my questions again.
Jeffrey Lorenger
Chairman, President, and CEO, HNI
No problem. Thanks, Budd.
Operator
That does conclude our question and answer session. At this time, I'd like to turn the conference back over to Jeffrey Lorenger for closing remarks.
Jeffrey Lorenger
Chairman, President, and CEO, HNI
Yeah. Thank you. I'd like to thank everybody for your interest in HNI and joining us today on the call, and have a great rest of your day. Thanks.
Operator
That does conclude today's conference call. You may now disconnect.
